_note: WhatsDaf's own English renderings of the Hebrew commentaries on Sefaria (Vilna edition). Keys are <commentary>:<amud><segment>.<comment>. Square brackets are our clarifications. Very long Tosafot are condensed and marked "In brief".
rashi:a1.1: And afterward his daughter died: before he came to court to testify.
gershom:a1.1: And his daughter died: so he became distant [no longer a relative].
gershom:a2.1: Whoever’s beginning and end are in a state of fitness is fit, even though he was unfit in between.
gershom:a3.1: The Merciful One made it depend on seeing and telling: only that he be fit at the time of seeing and at the time of telling; even though he became unfit in between, we do not mind. [And there is: he is fit at both.]
tosafot:a2.1: “But why do I need ‘he’? According to Rabbi, as he holds; according to the Rabbis, as they hold” [the Gemara’s answer on 17b about “and if he is poor”]: And it is difficult: what do the Rabbis expound from the “he” here, “But if he is too poor for your valuation” (Leviticus 27:8)? Perhaps there is an exposition of this “he” somewhere, and we expound it [from there].
gershom:a4.1: “And he” is a witness: why do I need it?
rashi:a3.2: One might have thought they would be liable: the witnesses, [to bring] the offering for an oath of testimony, if they did not testify for him.
rashi:a3.3: But he did not single out his witnesses: for he adjured all of them.
gershom:a5.1: The verse states “and he is a witness”: [until] the witness hears the sound of the oath singled out [to him], and not that he joins him together with others.
rashi:a4.1: One might have thought that even if he said “whoever”: “Whoever knows testimony, I adjure him,” they would not be liable.
gershom:a6.1: One might have thought that even if he said “whoever”: “Whoever among you knows the testimony shall be under oath.”
rashi:a4.2: The verse states “and he is a witness,” and he did single out his witnesses: for he adjured only his witnesses.
gershom:a7.1: The verse states “and he is a witness,” and he did single out his witnesses: for he adjured his witnesses and not others.
gershom:a8.1: But with offerings it is not so: if he was poor and became rich, he does not bring a rich man’s offering.
gershom:a9.1: Rather, even if his father died at the time he is obligated to bring the offering and left him ten thousand litra, or his ship is at sea and comes to him with tens of thousands in rent, the Temple treasury has nothing [in them], and he brings a poor man’s offering.
gershom:a10.1: What is different about offerings, where the Temple treasury has nothing in them, and what is different about valuations, where one who was poor and became rich gives a rich man’s valuation? Because with offerings it is written, “whose means do not suffice for his purification” (Leviticus 14:32): if he has the means at the time of purification, yes; if not, no. But with valuations it is written, “according to the means of him who vowed shall the priest valuate him” (Leviticus 27:8): whenever he has the means, he gives a rich man’s valuation. And what we say below (24a), that a pearl is not held back for the light [the poor], etc., applies only when he has nothing [else]; but when he has something, he waits and gives a rich man’s valuation.
rashi:a5.1: He is wealthy: so why does the Temple treasury have nothing of them?
gershom:a11.1: His father died at the time of bringing the offering: then he is wealthy. Why does he bring a poor man’s offering?
rashi:a5.2: Leaving: his father has not yet died, but he is going to leave it to him.
gershom:a12.1: Say “leaving him”: that is, do not say “he died and left him,” so that it already came into his hands; rather, his father is leaving [it to him].
rashi:a6.1: It is obvious: for he does not have it.
gershom:a13.1: It is obvious: that the Temple treasury has nothing, since it has not yet reached his hands.
rashi:a6.2: Where his father was moribund: at the time the priest valuates him.
tosafot:a6.1: “It is necessary only where his father was moribund,” etc.: The Kuntres [Rashi] explained: but with valuations, the Merciful One made it depend on the priest’s judgment, and if he sees that the father is moribund, he does not valuate him until his father dies. This is not plausible, for below we say that the Temple treasury has only its place and its time; and just after this too the Gemara cites, “You compared assessments to valuations, and a pearl to the light,” meaning a poor man who valuated himself and has a pearl now worth only twenty sela: we do not say, “Let us wait until market day, when it will rise to fifty sela”; rather we assess it as it is now, and he gives only twenty sela. If so, why should we need to wait until his father dies? Therefore Ri holds that “but with offerings it is not so” does not refer to “his father died”; rather it refers to what was said before it, and it is the end of Rabbi Yehuda’s statement. And what is explained afterward, “even if his father died and left him,” etc., is a matter of its own, in which offerings and valuations are the same.
gershom:a14.1: [Lest you say] most moribund people go on to die: and it is as though he had died, so that it has already reached his hands and he is wealthy. It teaches us [that it is not so].
rashi:a7.1: Where it was [leased]: his ship was leased in the hands of others, and he has nothing in it except its rent; and that is the “ten thousand” the mishna speaks of.
gershom:a15.1: [Where it was] leased: [leased] for half the profit or for a third.
gershom:a16.1: Rent is [paid only at the end]: and it has not yet reached his hands, so he is not wealthy.
gershom:a17.1: [But let him derive it due to the ship: the ship itself, which is his, so he is wealthy.]
rashi:a8.1: Whose is this? It is Rabbi Eliezer’s: who says below, in the chapter Shum HaYetomim (Arakhin 23b), regarding valuations: if he was a donkey driver, the priest leaves him his donkey and does not take it for the Temple treasury.
gershom:a18.1: Whose is this: that we do not count it?
rashi:a8.2: His pair: a pair of oxen, which is his livelihood.
gershom:a19.1: It is Rabbi Elazar’s [so Rabbeinu Gershom’s text; the daf reads Rabbi Eliezer]: who says below, regarding one who consecrates his property, that if he was a farmer [they leave him his pair]; so too here, if he was a sailor, he is left his ship.
rashi:a9.1: Mishna. A youth: [one] from twenty to sixty years old, whose valuation is fifty shekels.
gershom:a20.1: [The years follow the one vowed: they make the time of the years depend on the one vowed, not on the one who makes the vow, as it explains: How so? A youth who valuated an elder, etc.]
rashi:a9.2: The valuations follow the one valuated: and in fixing the amount of the valuation we do not follow the one who valuates.
gershom:a21.1: The valuation at the time of the valuation: they make the valuation depend on the time he valuated. How so? He valuated [someone] less than five years old, and did not manage to give the valuation before he became more than five; or less than twenty, etc.: he gives only what he was obligated to give at the time he valuated.
rashi:a11.1: Gemara. You compared assessments to valuations: in the first chapter (above, 4b), where we say: “He vowed” with “by your valuation of persons”: “vowed” refers to assessments, “by your valuation” refers to valuations; the verse compared them for these two matters.
gershom:a22.1: You compared it: for it is written regarding an impure animal, “and the priest shall valuate it” (Leviticus 27:12), yet there is no valuation for an animal, only assessment, as it is written, “according to your valuation, so it shall stand.” Why, then, does it express it in the language of valuations? To compare assessments to valuations for these laws: a pearl for the light, as it says in the chapter Shum HaYetomim [on] “and he shall give your valuation on that day,” that he should not hold it back.
rashi:a11.2: A pearl for the light: for with a pearl we follow the light [the poor], as it is written regarding valuations, “and he shall give your valuation on that day” (Leviticus 27:23), and we expound below (24a) that a pearl is not held back for the light. A poor man valuated himself, and the priest came to valuate him, and he has a pearl worth thirty sela. We do not say: if it is kept until it is brought up to a city where there is a rich man who would buy it for fifty sela, then he has fifty sela and should give a full valuation. We do not say so; the Temple treasury has only its place and its time. So too with assessments: if one said, “The value of this pearl is upon me,” we do not assess it by the sale price in the cities, but by the price at that time and in that place.
gershom:a23.1: A pearl for the light: that is, a light, poor person who consecrated his property and had a fine pearl. We do not assess it at what it would be worth in the hands of a rich man who can wait, or at the high price for which one who brought it up to such-and-such a city would sell it; rather, the Temple treasury has only what it is worth in the place of the one consecrating and at his time, for we do not wait for market day for it to be sold at a high price. [And likewise a cow is not held for the butchers’ market.] So for this assessments were compared to valuations: that it has only [its value] at the time of the valuation.
rashi:a11.3: And to assess it by its significance: that if he valuated something on which life depends, for instance he said, “The valuation of my head is upon me,” he gives a full valuation, as it is written regarding valuations, “by your valuation of persons,” so we follow the person [as a whole].
gershom:a24.1: And to assess it by its significance: that if he said, “The value of my head,” or “of my liver, is upon me,” it is assessed by the significance of the limb, as with valuations, and he gives the value of all of him, because life depends on it.
rashi:a12.1: That he gives according to the time of giving: for with assessments it is obvious to us that he gives according to the time of giving and not the time of the vow, since he is assessed like a slave in the market. If he said, “My value is upon me,” in Tishrei, and came to court in Nisan, who knows what he was worth at the time of the vow? And the time of giving is the time he comes to court.
tosafot:a12.1: That he gives according to the time of giving: Rashi explained that with assessments it is obvious to the Gemara that he gives according to the time of giving and not the time of the vow, since he is assessed like a slave in the market; and if he said, “My value is upon me,” in Tishrei and came to court in Nisan, who knows what he was worth at the time of the vow? And the time of giving is the time he comes to court. So far Rashi’s words. This is puzzling: what reasoning is this? Why should we say he was worth more than now? And if we see that he is weak now and was strong then, we certainly know he was worth more then, and we would be causing the Temple treasury a loss, since we see he was worth at least a sela more. Therefore Ri says this is not a matter of reasoning; rather there is some proof from a verse for it. Furthermore, we learned below, in the chapter HaOmer Mishkali (Arakhin 20a): if the one whose value was vowed died, the heirs do not give, because the dead have no value. If the reason were from reasoning, that we follow the time of giving, that reasoning would not apply there, for we know he was worth at least a sela while alive; so why do we exempt the heirs entirely? Rather, there is certainly some verse for it.
gershom:a25.1: One might have thought we should compare valuations to assessments: that he gives according to the time of giving, as it is written, “and he shall give your valuation on that day” (Leviticus 27:23); and this “your valuation” means assessments, as we said above.
rashi:a12.2: The verse states “according to your valuation it shall stand”: which implies valuations by the time of the valuation; so that if he valuated himself at sixty and became more than sixty, he gives the large valuation and not the valuation of an elder.
gershom:a26.1: The verse states “according to your valuation, so it shall stand”: it stands as at the time of the valuation.
rashi:a13.1: Mishna. The thirtieth day is like below it: if he said, “The valuation of this little one is upon me,” and that little one was thirty days old that day, it is like below, and he has said nothing; for there is no valuation for one less than a month old, as it is written, “And if from a month old…” (Leviticus 27:6).
gershom:a27.1: [The thirtieth day is like below it: if he valuated on the thirtieth day, it is as if he valuated one less than a month old, and he gives nothing.]
rashi:a13.2: And upward: implies that the sixtieth year has been completed, and then he is judged as an elder; but in the sixtieth year he is judged as a youth.
gershom:a28.1: The fifth year and the twentieth year are like below them: if he valuated in the fifth year, he gives the valuation of one from thirty days [the first bracket], as if he had valuated in the third or fourth year, as it is written, “And if from a month old until five years old.” And so the twentieth year is like below it, so that he gives the valuation of one from five years. As it is stated, “And if from sixty years old and upward”: since it is written “sixty years old” and it needed to write “and upward,” learn from it that what one valuates from sixty onward is like above, but the sixtieth year itself is like below it.
rashi:a14.1: Is that so? If we made: said as a question. That is: is it so? If we made the sixtieth year like below, that is to be stringent, for one younger than sixty has a large valuation of fifty sela, and one older than sixty has a valuation of only fifteen sela.
gershom:a29.1: [And we learn them all from the sixtieth year, etc. Is that so? If he makes the sixtieth year like below, that is to be stringent, for from twenty to sixty the valuation is fifty shekels and from sixty upward it is only fifteen shekels. Shall we make the fifth year and the twentieth year like below to be lenient? For below five the valuation is not as great as that of five, and likewise below twenty the valuation is smaller than above twenty.]
gershom:a30.1: The verse states “year,” “year”: “year” is stated with sixty, [and] “year” with five and with twenty, for a verbal analogy; that is, it is a comparison [set by the verse], and one does not refute such a comparison, whether to be lenient or to be stringent.
rashi:a15.1: To be lenient: for the valuation of one [older] than twenty is larger than that of one younger than twenty, and so too with five, as written in the verses.
rashi:a15.2: Rabbi Eliezer says: the fifth year, the twentieth year and the sixtieth year are always like below, until the whole year is complete and a month and one day of the next year [have passed].
gershom:a31.1: [Rabbi Eliezer says: until they are a month and one day beyond the years: so that he never gives the valuation of one five years old until he is five and a month and one day beyond five; and likewise he never gives the valuation of one twenty years old until he is twenty and a month and one day.]
rashi:a16.1: Gemara. It could be refuted as we refuted it: in the mishna.
gershom:a32.1: Free: this “year,” “year” is not needed for itself but to be used for the verbal analogy; for otherwise it could be refuted as we refuted in the mishna: “Is that so? If he made the sixtieth year like below,” etc.
rashi:a16.2: The words “year” are superfluous: for it could have written, “And if from five years old until twenty,” and I would know that “twenty” too speaks of years. Why do I need “year”? And so with “sixty.”
gershom:a33.1: [The words “year,” “year” are written superfluously; that is, why] do I need it to write “year” with the twentieth year and with the [sixtieth] year? Let it be learned from “five years old”! Rather, it is for the comparison.
gershom:a34.1: And some explain [that the superfluous] “year” (and so Rashi explained, in the comment beginning “the words ‘year’ are superfluous”) is the extra “years,” for it could have said, “And if from five years old until twenty,” and would not have needed to write the latter “years”; and all of them are the latter “year.” [The text of this note is partly garbled.]
rashi:a17.1: Let us say the mishna: which needs a verse to teach that the twentieth year is like below, is not in accordance with Rabbi. For if it were Rabbi’s, he says “until” means until and including; and since it is written, “from five years old until twenty,” I would know on my own that the twentieth year is included, which is “like below.”
gershom:a35.1: For if it were Rabbi’s, he says below that “until” means until and including; that is, since it wrote “until five years old” and “until twenty years old,” we would understand on our own that it is like below it, for “until” means until and including, and the verbal analogy would not be needed.
rashi:a18.1: One might have thought: that from the first day onward he is warned against leaven, and the first is not included.
tosafot:a18.1: One might have thought: the first but not including the first, the seventh but not including the seventh: And if you ask, how is it possible to say so? Isn’t it written, “Seven days you shall eat matzot” (Exodus 13:6)? One can answer that it speaks of liability to karet, for karet is written in this verse, as it is written, “For whoever eats leavened bread, that soul shall be cut off … from the first day until the seventh day” (Exodus 12:15). That is why it cites, “The verse states: until the twenty-first day in the evening,” and karet is also written with that verse.
gershom:a36.1: His head and not including his head, until his feet and not including his feet: because it is written, “as far as the priest can see” (Leviticus 13:12), and his head and his feet are not examined together in a single look.
rashi:b1.1: Like the matter that is stated, “from his head to his feet”: which is obvious to us, as is explained below: “from his head” and not including his head.
rashi:b2.1: The verse states, “until the twenty-first day of the month in the evening”: so the first day is included, as written at the beginning of the verse, “in the evening you shall eat matzot,” and the seventh is also included, from the end of the verse, as it is written, “in the evening.”
gershom:b1.1: The verse states, “until the twenty-first day of the month in the evening”: at the end of the days, meaning that the first and the seventh are included.
gershom:b2.1: Rabbi says: It is not necessary: rather, since it is written, “from the first day until the seventh day,” both are included, and no verbal analogy is needed.
rashi:b3.1: The verses offset each other: the expositions are evenly balanced. By Rabbi’s exposition, one could decide [the fifth year] as like below and one could decide it as like above. For it is written, “from a month old until five years old, then your valuation…,” and we say “until” is until and including, so five is like below. Then it is written, “And if from five years old until twenty…,” and according to Rabbi, “from five” includes five, since he says that “from the first day” means the first is included; so the fifth year is like above. Therefore, without the verbal analogy we would have no decision either way.
gershom:b3.1: The verses offset each other: for we do not know whether to say “until” is until and including or not; for just as it implies below, so it implies above. How so? If we say, “And if from a month old until five years old,” it implies that the fifth year is included [in that bracket]; but it is also written, “And if from five years old until twenty years old,” which implies that the fifth year is like above it, up to twenty. Therefore a verbal analogy is needed.
rashi:b3.2: Why do I need “from five” as well: it should have written thus: “and until twenty years old, then your valuation…,” and “until sixty years old, then your valuation….”
rashi:b4.1: The signs of his body are different from the signs of his head: for the signs of a mark in a place of hair [the head] are judged by yellow hair, and of a mark in a place of flesh by white hair and by spreading.
gershom:b4.1: That is why we do not say his head is included and his feet are included: for the signs of his body are different from the signs of his head. The signs of his body are judged by white hair and by spreading, and the signs of his head are judged by yellow hair.
rashi:b4.2: As far as the priest can see: and he cannot see on the head because of the hair, nor on the foot between toe and toe.
tosafot:b4.1: Alternatively, say: “As far as the priest can see”: he cannot see on the head because of the hair, nor on the foot between toe and toe. And if you ask: here it implies that [the rule of a mark that] spread over all of him does not apply to the foot, yet in Eizehu Mekoman (Zevaḥim 49b) it does not imply so. For there Rabbi Natan ben Avtolemos says: From where is it derived that [a mark that] spread over all of a garment is pure? “Baldness of the back” and “baldness of the front” are stated with garments, and “baldness of the back” and “baldness of the front” are stated with a person; just as there, if it spread over all of him he is pure, so too here, if it spread over all of it, it is pure. And there, from where do we derive it? For it is written, “from his head to his feet”: just as there, [at] his foot, if all of it turned [white] he is pure, so too here, [at] his head, if all of it turned [white] he is pure. [This implies] that spreading does apply to the foot, since it derives the head from the foot.
gershom:b5.1: As far as the priest can see: and the priest’s eyes cannot take in his head and his feet in one look.
rashi:b5.1: And it is stated there: regarding the Levites, “a month old and upward.” Just as there it means a month and one day, as it is written, “from a month old and upward,” meaning he has already entered the next month, so too here, a month and one day.
tosafot:b5.1: “And his redeemed, from a month old and upward” [so Tosafot’s text of the Gemara]: We searched for this verse and did not find it, only “and his redeemed, from a month old shall you redeem” (Numbers 18:16). Perhaps it expounds this from what is written, “and his redeemed, from a month old,” which implies from a month old and upward, since it did not write “a month old.”
gershom:b6.1: Just as there: a month and one day, for “and upward” is written there.
rashi:b6.1: Just as there it is one day: just as “upward” written with “a month” is only one day, so too “upward” here, with years, is only one day.
gershom:b7.1: Just as there it is one day: more than what is written in the Torah, as it is written, “and his redeemed, from a month old shall you redeem” (Numbers 18:16); so too here, one day, so that they are only one day beyond the years.
rashi:b6.2: What purpose does the verbal analogy serve: without the verbal analogy I would know that we require one day, since “and upward” is written.
gershom:b8.1: [If so, what purpose does the verbal analogy serve? Rather, the verbal analogy comes for this: a month and one day.]
rashi:b7.1: A year stated with regard to consecrated animals: for example, “lambs in their first year” (Numbers 28:3).
rashi:b7.2: Two years of an ancestral field: one who sells an ancestral field may not redeem it until it has been two years in the buyer’s hands, as it is written, “according to the number of years of the crops he shall sell to you” (Leviticus 25:15–16), and the minimum of “years” is two.
gershom:b9.1: [All of them] from time to time: [twelve months] from day to day, and not [a year] by the world’s count; for by the world’s count, from Tishrei until Nisan would already count for him as a year.
tosafot:b8.1: In brief: “Its own year, and not the year of the world.” Rabbi Shmuel ben Rabbi Elḥanan asked: why is a verse needed? It follows from reasoning: otherwise, how could lambs for the daily offering ever be fit on Rosh HaShana? One born before Rosh HaShana would be in its second year as soon as Rosh HaShana came, while the daily offering requires a lamb in its first year; and one born on Rosh HaShana is too young to be offered. Some answer that an animal’s year is counted only from the day it becomes fit to be accepted, as is said of the firstborn, “year by year” (Rosh HaShana 6b), and so too here. Tosafot rejects this: that count applies only to the prohibition of delaying, not to counting an animal’s age, since Zevaḥim 25b rules that hours disqualify consecrated animals (a lamb slaughtered on the day its year ends, before the hour of its birth, whose blood was sprinkled only after that hour, is disqualified), which could never happen if we counted from fitness; so we count from the actual birth, and the question returns. [The author’s] teacher, Rabbi Shmuel, answers that the verse is still needed, for without it we would not count from time to time [to the hour] here, as stated in the last chapter (Arakhin 31a). Open on Sefaria for the full text.
rashi:b10.1: Years of the crops: since it writes “years,” “years of the crops,” why do I need “crops”? Rather, it teaches that every crop he finds in those two years he eats, even three. For instance, if he sold it to him in Nisan, full of standing grain, [the seller] may not redeem it until two years later, in Nisan, on that same day; and if [the buyer] hurried and reaped, he has eaten three crops. When the seller redeems it, he calculates the years from the day he sold it until the Jubilee: if there were ten years and he sold it for ten maneh, it turns out he sold it at a maneh for each year, since at the Jubilee it was going to return. Therefore, when he redeems it now, he gives eight maneh for the eight remaining years, and this one has eaten three crops worth several maneh in two years. Whereas if we followed the world’s count, from Tishrei of the following year he could redeem it, and [the buyer] would have eaten only two crops.
tosafot:b10.1: “According to the number of years of the crops”: sometimes a person eats three crops in two years. And if you ask, how do we expound this from this verse? Say rather four crops, since “years” implies two and “crops” implies two, so there are four! One can answer that it expounds from “number,” which implies [the number of] years [that is, two]; and it should have written “crop” [in the singular]; [writing “crops”] implies that there is one more crop. And Ri found it difficult: even if we count by the years of the world, one finds three crops in two years; for instance, if he sold him a field full of produce on the second of Tishrei, then when Tishrei two years later comes, he has already reaped its produce by the twenty-ninth of Elul. One can answer that three crops in two years are more common when we count from time to time than when we count from the creation of the world.
gershom:b10.1: Sometimes a person eats [three crops in two years]: for instance, he sold it to him before Rosh HaShana when it was full of produce. He eats this produce, sows it and eats produce from it before one Rosh HaShana, [and again] sows it and eats produce from it until [the next] Rosh HaShana; so he eats three crops in two years. Whereas if we followed the years of the world, since he sold it to him before Rosh HaShana, once the next Rosh HaShana came [and the one after it], the two years would already be over.
tosafot:b11.1: “And in the seventh” he shall also work: Rabbi Y. ben Yom Tov asked: we learn from here only [counting] from time to time for the last year; but from time to time for the other years, from where do we derive it? Say that thirty days before Rosh HaShana count as a year! And the Rashbam answered him that the verse “and in the seventh” revealed this to us about the last year, and the same holds for the other years: we follow from time to time with them, like these others that are written.
gershom:b11.1: “Six years he shall work, and in the seventh”: which implies that he also works in the seventh, for the “and” adds to the first matter, when he bought him in the middle of the first year.
rashi:b12.1: And those of a son and a daughter: years stated regarding a son and a daughter; and below it explains them.
rashi:b12.2: From time to time: that same day and that same hour in the next year; and we do not follow the world’s count, counting it a year when Tishrei arrives.
rashi:b12.3: For valuations: that for the fifth, twentieth and sixtieth years we do not follow the world’s count.
tosafot:b12.1: For valuations: And if you ask, with valuations, from where do we derive that we require from time to time? Ri explained that we derive it from “a month old”: just as one is not valuated as a month old unless he has a full month, for one cannot say we follow the month of the world, so too for all the others, five years old and twenty years old.
gershom:b12.1: [For valuations: the five years, twenty and sixty years stated in valuations are all from time to time.]
rashi:b12.4: For the chapter Yotze Dofen: in tractate Nidda (45b): a boy of twelve years, his vows are examined; of thirteen, his vows stand; a girl of eleven, her vows are examined; of twelve, her vows stand. Many years of a son and a daughter are taught there likewise, and it says here that all of them are from time to time from when they were born.
gershom:b13.1: For the chapter Yotze Dofen: of tractate Nidda, where we learned: a girl three years and one day old, a boy nine years and one day old, a girl eleven years and one day, a girl twelve years and one day, a boy twelve years, a boy thirteen years. All these years are from time to time.
gershom:b14.1: Do you dispute: you and Rav Giddel, so that you do not hold like Rav Giddel?
gershom:b15.1: We do not dispute: I said one thing in Rav’s name, and he said one thing.
rashi:b13.1: But doesn’t Rav say: there, in tractate Nidda (47b).
rashi:b13.2: The halakha in the entire chapter: of Yotze Dofen is from time to time.
rashi:b14.1: What is the reason he did not say Yotze Dofen: since he too holds there that it is from time to time.
rashi:b14.2: He would tell you: even so, it does not teach them here, for it teaches [cases] similar to these, the year of consecrated animals and of a Hebrew slave, which are written in the Torah; while those years of Yotze Dofen are all rabbinic.
gershom:b16.1: Similar to these: houses of walled cities, an ancestral field, a Hebrew slave [and valuations], which are written explicitly in the Torah.
gershom:b17.1: If it enters your mind: that it includes valuations because they are written.
